x: The Election Commission is a permanent, independent constitutional body under Part XV, Articles 324–329. Articles 243K and 243ZA (Part IX) cover the State Election Commissions.
t: Recall Part XV and Articles 324 to 329.

x: The Election Commission was set up on 25 January 1950, a day before the Republic. Since 2011, 25 January has been National Voters' Day.
t: Discriminate 25 January 1950 (Commission) from 26 January (Republic).

x: Option B is incorrect: Panchayat and municipal elections are run by State Election Commissions (Articles 243K, 243ZA). The ECI runs Parliament, State Legislature, President and Vice-President elections.
t: Discriminate the ECI's elections from the State commissions'.

x: Both are true: the CEC and the two Election Commissioners have equal powers, and they decide by majority. Majority voting does not explain equal powers, so R does not explain A.
t: Ask whether the voting rule explains equal powers.

x: Article 324 sets up the ECI, 243K the State Election Commission for Panchayats, 243ZA for municipalities, and 326 adult suffrage. The answer is a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Recall Articles 324, 326, 243K and 243ZA.

x: Option B is incorrect: the Governor has no role in removing the CEC, who can be removed only like a Supreme Court judge. Other Election Commissioners and Regional Commissioners are removed by the President on the CEC's recommendation.
t: Recall the CEC's removal safeguard.

x: Both are true: the President decides MPs' disqualification on the ECI's binding opinion (Article 103), and the Governor does the same for State legislators (Article 192).
t: Pair Article 103 (MPs) with Article 192 (State legislators).

x: I, II and III are correct: Article 325 provides one electoral roll with no discrimination, and Article 326 adult suffrage. IV is false because Kuldip Nayar (2006) held the right to vote statutory, not fundamental.
t: Remember that the right to vote is statutory.

x: The 61st Amendment (1988) lowered the voting age from 21 to 18, effective from 1989.
t: Recall the 61st Amendment.

x: Both are true: the Model Code of Conduct is not a law of Parliament because it is a set of ECI guidelines that apply once elections are announced. R explains A.
t: Ask whether being an ECI guideline explains not being an Act.

x: The first EVM was used at Parur (1982), EPIC cards came in 1993, VVPAT on 4 September 2013 and NOTA on 27 September 2013. The order is C, A, B, D.
t: Recall the dates 1982, 1993, and 4 and 27 September 2013.

x: Under Section 33(7) of the RPA, 1951, a candidate can contest from at most two constituencies, a limit added in 1996.
t: Recall the two-constituency limit.

x: Both are true: Article 324(1) gives the ECI superintendence, direction and control of elections, and Article 324 is in Part XV. Its location does not explain its content, so R does not explain A.
t: Ask whether an Article's location explains its content.

x: The ECI has one CEC and two Election Commissioners, all appointed by the President, each serving six years or to age 65. The answer is a-iv, b-ii, c-iii, d-i.
t: Recall the ECI's size, appointment and tenure.

x: All three are correct: the ECI has been a three-member body continuously since 1 October 1993, and its members are paid like Supreme Court judges.
t: Recall the 1993 change to a multi-member Commission.

x: Article 324(5) protects the CEC: they can be removed only like a Supreme Court judge.
t: Recall Article 324(5).

x: Article 243K sets up State Election Commissions for Panchayats and 243ZA for municipalities. 243K is in Part IX and 243ZA in Part IX-A. The answer is a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Pair Article 243K (Part IX) with 243ZA (Part IX-A).

x: Six are run by the ECI: the Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha, Assembly, Council, President and Vice-President elections. The three Panchayat tiers are run by the State Election Commission.
t: Discriminate the ECI's elections from the State commissions'.

x: Municipal and corporation elections are run by the State Election Commission. The CEC is removed like a Supreme Court judge, and a State Election Commissioner like a High Court judge. The answer is a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
t: Discriminate the two removal safeguards.

x: Both are true: each State Election Commission works under that State's Panchayat and municipal laws.
t: Recall the State Election Commission's legal basis.

x: The right to vote is a legal or statutory right, under the RP Acts, not a fundamental right. Adult suffrage (Article 326) is the principle, not the right's category.
t: Remember that the right to vote is statutory.

x: The ECI registers parties under the RPA, 1951, allots symbols under the Symbols Order, 1968, and settles party mergers and splits. The answer is a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Discriminate registration (RPA 1951) from recognition and symbols (1968 Order).

x: All three are correct: a party becomes a national party by meeting any one of them: 2% of Lok Sabha seats from three States, or 6% of votes in four States plus four seats, or State-party status in four States.
t: Recall the three routes to national-party status.

x: Both are true: the President notifies elections to Parliament and the Governor notifies State Legislature elections, on the ECI's recommendation.
t: Discriminate who notifies elections from who conducts them.

x: The ECI recommends dates and sets the schedule, the President or Governor notifies, and a Delimitation Commission set up by law redraws constituencies. The answer is a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv, e-v.
t: Note that two List-I items name each body twice.

x: Both are true: Delimitation Commission orders cannot be challenged in court, and legislatures cannot change them. These are two separate safeguards, so R does not explain A.
t: Ask whether two parallel safeguards explain each other.

x: A candidate loses the security deposit if they win no more than one-sixth of the valid votes.
t: Recall the one-sixth rule.

x: VVPAT was introduced at Noksen (Nagaland), Sukumar Sen was the first CEC (1950–58), and V.S. Ramadevi the first woman CEC (1990). The answer is a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv, e-v.
t: Recall each first and its date.

x: All five could need amending for simultaneous elections: Articles 83 and 85 (Parliament's term and sessions), 172 and 174 (the States'), and 356 (President's Rule).
t: Recall the Articles on the terms of the Houses.

x: Under Article 324, the Election Commission of India conducts elections to the offices of President and Vice-President, to Parliament and to State Legislatures.
t: Recall the ECI's four kinds of election.

x: Under Articles 243K and 243ZA, State Election Commissions conduct Panchayat and municipal elections. Parliament and the Legislatures are the ECI's.
t: Discriminate the ECI's elections from the State commissions'.

x: Option C is incorrect: the Legislative Council elects its own Chairman under Article 182. Presiding officers are chosen by their own Houses, not by the ECI.
t: Recall that each House elects its own presiding officers.

x: A is true: election disputes go only to the courts, through election petitions. B is false because disputes over the President's and Vice-President's elections go to the Supreme Court (Article 71).
t: Recall Article 71.

x: The right to vote and the right to stand for election are both legal or statutory rights, not fundamental rights.
t: Remember that both electoral rights are statutory.

x: The President is elected by elected MPs and MLAs, and the Vice-President by all MPs, both by single transferable vote. The Lok Sabha is directly elected by first-past-the-post, and the Rajya Sabha by elected MLAs. The answer is a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
t: Compare who votes in each election.

x: All three are correct: nominated members and MLCs cannot vote for the President, and a candidate needs 50 proposers and 50 seconders.
t: Recall who is left out of the Presidential electoral college.

x: Both are true: the Vice-President is elected only by MPs (elected and nominated), which is why State Legislatures have no role. R explains A.
t: Contrast the Vice-President's electoral college with the President's.

x: Option C is incorrect: under first-past-the-post, the candidate with the most votes wins, even without 50%. It is used for the Lok Sabha.
t: Discriminate a plurality from an absolute majority.

x: All four are correct: a Legislative Council has one-third elected by MLAs and one-third by local bodies, one-twelfth by graduates (and one-twelfth by teachers), and one-sixth nominated by the Governor.
t: Check that the fractions add up to one.

x: Option A is incorrect: industrialists are not an electorate for the Council. The electorates are MLAs, local bodies, graduates and teachers, chosen by single transferable vote. The minimum age is 30.
t: Recall the Council's four electorates.

x: Assembly members are directly elected by the State's voters through first-past-the-post. Indirect election by single transferable vote is for the Rajya Sabha and the Council.
t: Discriminate direct elections from indirect ones.

x: Three are correct: the minimum age is 30 for Council members and 21 for local bodies, and the 61st Amendment lowered the voting age to 18. Statement 3 is false because the voting age is 18.
t: Recall the ages 18, 21, 25 and 30.

x: A is true: ward members and panches are directly elected by local voters. B is false because local elections are run by the State Election Commission.
t: Discriminate the ECI's elections from the State commissions'.

x: The 70th Amendment (1992) added the elected MLAs of Delhi and Puducherry to the electoral college for the President.
t: Recall the 70th Amendment.

x: Both are true: under Article 71(4), vacancies in the electoral college do not invalidate or delay a Presidential election. R explains A.
t: Recall Article 71(4).

x: Both are true: an MLA's vote value depends on their State's population, while every MP's vote has the same value.
t: Discriminate MLAs' vote values (vary) from MPs' (equal).

x: Both are true: the President is elected by single transferable vote, and voting is by secret ballot. The ballot is a method, not the reason for the system, so R does not explain A.
t: Ask whether a voting method explains an electoral system.

x: A is true: Lok Sabha members are directly elected from territorial constituencies. B is false because the Lok Sabha uses first-past-the-post, not single transferable vote.
t: Discriminate first-past-the-post from proportional representation.

x: Option A is incorrect: Rajya Sabha seats are shared among States by population (Fourth Schedule), not equally. Elected MLAs choose them, and the House is set up under Article 80.
t: Recall that Rajya Sabha seats follow population.

x: A is true: the Vice-President is the Rajya Sabha's ex-officio Chairman. B is false because the Vice-President is not a member of it.
t: Discriminate presiding over a House from being a member of it.

x: Article 326 provides adult suffrage: every citizen aged 18 or over can vote in Lok Sabha and Assembly elections.
t: Recall Article 326.

x: I and II are correct: nominated MLAs and MLCs cannot vote in Rajya Sabha elections. III is false because those elections are indirect, by elected MLAs.
t: Recall who votes in Rajya Sabha elections.

x: The President is elected indirectly by the electoral college, the Vice-President by all MPs, the Lok Sabha directly, and the Rajya Sabha by elected MLAs. The answer is a-iv, b-ii, c-i, d-iii.
t: Compare who votes in each election.

x: I, II and III are correct: one-sixth of the Council is nominated, and graduates and teachers each elect one-twelfth. IV is false because industrialists are not an electorate.
t: Recall the Council's four electorates.

x: All five are correct: the President is elected under Article 54, the Vice-President under 66, the Lok Sabha under 81, the Assembly under 170 and the Council under 171.
t: Recall each body's main Article.

x: Legislative Council elections are by secret ballot, with single transferable vote. Direct election and first-past-the-post belong to the Assembly.
t: Recall how Council elections are held.

x: The RPA, 1950 covers seat allocation, delimitation, who can vote and electoral rolls. The RPA, 1951 covers conducting elections, candidates and disputes.
t: Discriminate the 1950 Act (before polls) from the 1951 Act (the polls themselves).

x: Option B is incorrect: corrupt practices come under the RPA, 1951, along with party registration and election petitions. The 1950 Act covers seats, rolls and the composition of Councils.
t: Discriminate the 1950 Act (before polls) from the 1951 Act (the polls themselves).

x: Both are true: the ECI registers political parties because Section 29A of the RPA, 1951 gives it that power. R explains A.
t: Recall Section 29A.

x: A is false: the right to vote is statutory, not fundamental. B is true: the right to contest is also statutory (Kuldip Nayar, 2006).
t: Remember that both electoral rights are statutory.

x: I and II are correct: the RPA, 1950 links to Articles 81, 82, 170, 171, 325 and 326, and the 1951 Act to 84, 102, 173, 191, 324 and 329. III is false because Article 329 belongs with the 1951 Act.
t: Match each Act to its Articles.

x: The RPA, 1950 sets the pre-election framework and rolls, the 1951 Act governs elections and candidates, Section 29A covers registration, and the 1968 Order recognition. The answer is a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.
t: Discriminate registration (Section 29A) from recognition (1968 Order).

x: Under Section 33(7) of the RPA, 1951, a candidate can contest from at most two constituencies, Parliamentary or Assembly, at a time.
t: Recall the two-constituency limit.

x: Both are true: since a 2003 amendment removed the rule that a candidate must be a voter in that State, any registered voter in India can contest a Rajya Sabha seat from any State. R explains A.
t: Recall the 2003 change upheld in Kuldip Nayar.

x: Option A is incorrect: since the 1996 amendment, a candidate's death no longer cancels the election automatically. A recognised party can name a replacement within a set time.
t: Recall the 1996 change on a candidate's death.

x: The Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990) dealt with electoral reform, recommending State funding of elections and EVMs.
t: Recall the subject of the Goswami Committee.

x: The four Delimitation Commissions were set up in 1952, 1963, 1973 and 2002. The order is B, D, A, C.
t: Recall the years 1952, 1963, 1973 and 2002.

x: All three are routes to national-party status: 6% of votes in four States plus four Lok Sabha seats, or 2% of Lok Sabha seats from three States, or State-party status in four States.
t: Recall the three routes to national-party status.

x: The Model Code of Conduct takes effect as soon as the ECI announces the election schedule, and lasts until the results.
t: Recall when the Model Code starts.

x: Both are true: the RPA, 1950 sets seat quotas and the delimitation framework, and the 1951 Act covers party registration (Section 29A) and corrupt practices.
t: Discriminate the 1950 Act (before polls) from the 1951 Act (the polls themselves).

x: The RPA, 1951 covers the running of elections: nomination, scrutiny and counting. Seats, rolls and Council composition are in the 1950 Act.
t: Discriminate the 1950 Act (before polls) from the 1951 Act (the polls themselves).

x: I and II are correct: the RPA, 1950 covers voter registration and the 1951 Act disqualifications. III is false because corrupt practices are in the 1951 Act.
t: Discriminate the 1950 Act (before polls) from the 1951 Act (the polls themselves).

x: The RPA, 1950 covers seat quotas and delimitation, and the 1951 Act nomination, scrutiny and counting. The pre-election framework includes rolls, and the 1951 Act governs candidates. The answer is a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Discriminate the 1950 Act (before polls) from the 1951 Act (the polls themselves).

x: Both are true: the 1996 amendment capped contests at two constituencies after Devi Lal stood from three Lok Sabha seats in 1991. R explains A.
t: Recall the Devi Lal case behind the 1996 cap.

x: I, II and III are correct: the Goswami Committee recommended State funding of elections and EVMs, and its proposals led to the 1996 RPA amendment. IV is false because Council seat allocation was not its subject.
t: Recall the Goswami Committee's proposals.

x: The Delimitation Commission is set up under an Act of Parliament, headed by a retired Supreme Court judge, with the CEC and State Election Commissioners as members. The answer is a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
t: Recall the Delimitation Commission's members.

x: Option C is incorrect: Delimitation Commission orders have the force of law, cannot be challenged in court (Article 329), and cannot be changed when laid before Parliament or the Assemblies.
t: Recall the finality of delimitation orders.

x: A is true: the Centre sets up the Delimitation Commission under an Act of Parliament. B is false because a retired Supreme Court judge heads it, not a State Election Commissioner.
t: Recall who heads the Delimitation Commission.

x: Option B is incorrect: NOTA came from the Supreme Court's order in PUCL v. Union of India on 27 September 2013, not from the 1996 RPA amendment.
t: Recall the PUCL ruling of 2013.

x: I and II are correct: one route to national-party status is 2% of Lok Sabha seats, or 11 seats. III is false because those MPs must come from at least three States, not four.
t: Recall the three-State condition.

x: Article 84 covers qualifications for Parliament, 102 disqualifications for Parliament, 173 qualifications for State Legislatures, and 191 their disqualifications. The answer is a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Pair the Union Articles (84, 102) with the State ones (173, 191).

x: A is true: Kuldip Nayar (2006) upheld removing the rule that a Rajya Sabha candidate must be a voter in that State. B is false because the 2003 amendment removed that rule, not added it.
t: Recall the 2003 change upheld in Kuldip Nayar.

x: Both are true: the ECI registers political parties under Section 29A, not the Law Ministry or Parliament.
t: Recall Section 29A.

x: NOTA lets a voter reject all candidates by a secret negative vote. It does not force a fresh election even if NOTA tops the count.
t: Remember that NOTA is a symbolic rejection.

x: The Supreme Court ordered NOTA on EVMs in PUCL v. Union of India on 27 September 2013. Parur and Noksen are the first EVM and VVPAT sites.
t: Recall the PUCL ruling of 2013.

x: Both are true: the Court linked a secret negative vote to free expression, and Article 19(1)(a) is that freedom. R explains A.
t: Recall the Article behind NOTA.

x: The Electors Photo Identity Card (EPIC, the voter ID) was introduced in 1993. EVMs came in 1982 and VVPAT and NOTA in 2013.
t: Recall the order: EVM 1982, EPIC 1993, VVPAT and NOTA 2013.

x: NOTA means pressing a button on the EVM, old Rule 49-O meant refusing to vote before the presiding officer, and a full right to reject means rejecting all candidates on the ballot. The answer is a-ii, b-iii, c-i.
t: Contrast NOTA with Rule 49-O and the right to reject.

x: NOTA keeps secrecy fully (Article 19(1)(a)), Rule 49-O broke it by recording the refusal in Form 17-A, and a full right to reject keeps it. The answer is a-ii, b-iii, c-i.
t: Recall why Rule 49-O broke secrecy.

x: Under NOTA, the candidate with the most votes still wins, Rule 49-O did not affect the count, and a full right to reject forces a re-election above 50%. The answer is a-iii, b-ii, c-i.
t: Recall how each option affects the result.

x: Option C is incorrect: Rule 49-O never forced a re-election. The refusal did not affect the count, but recording it in Form 17-A broke secrecy, and the rule was struck down.
t: Recall what Rule 49-O did and why it fell.

x: Option D is incorrect: NOTA is only symbolic. Even if it tops the count, the candidate with the most votes wins and no fresh poll is held.
t: Remember that NOTA is a symbolic rejection.

x: A is true: using NOTA means voting, by registering a negative choice. B is false because NOTA is not the same as abstaining.
t: Discriminate a NOTA vote from abstention.

x: Option A is incorrect: the Supreme Court struck down NOTA for Rajya Sabha and Council elections in 2018. NOTA applies only to direct Lok Sabha and Assembly elections.
t: Recall the 2018 ruling on indirect elections.

x: Two happened in 2013: VVPAT at Noksen (4 September) and the NOTA ruling (27 September). EVMs were first used in 1982 and EPIC came in 1993.
t: Recall the order: EVM 1982, EPIC 1993, VVPAT and NOTA 2013.

x: EVM is Electronic Voting Machine, EPIC Electors Photo Identity Card, VVPAT Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail, and NOTA None of the Above. The answer is a-iv, b-ii, c-iii, d-i.
t: Expand each abbreviation.

x: Both are true: Rule 49-O was struck down because recording a voter's refusal in Form 17-A broke the secrecy of the vote. R explains A.
t: Ask whether the breach of secrecy explains the strike-down.

x: Both are true: VVPAT was introduced on 4 September 2013 and first used in the Noksen by-election in Nagaland.
t: Recall Noksen and 4 September 2013.

x: Option B is incorrect: India has no full right to reject. NOTA is only symbolic, while a full right to reject would force a re-election above 50%.
t: Contrast NOTA with the right to reject.

x: Three are features of NOTA: it is on ballots and EVMs, it lets voters reject all candidates in secret, and it is only symbolic. Statement 4 is false because NOTA does not apply to Rajya Sabha or Council elections.
t: Recall where NOTA applies.

x: An EVM is a machine that records and counts votes. It is not an electoral system; first-past-the-post is the system.
t: Discriminate a voting machine from an electoral system.

x: The nationwide rollout of voter ID cards (EPIC) began in 1993 under CEC T.N. Seshan.
t: Recall Seshan's 1993 reform.

x: Option C is incorrect: EVMs were first tried on 19 May 1982 at Parur in Kerala. 4 September 2013 is VVPAT's date. Goa was the first all-EVM State poll, and 2004 the first all-EVM general election.
t: Discriminate the EVM date (1982) from the VVPAT date (2013).

x: Both are true: EVMs are used under the ECI's superintendence, direction and control, which is the Article 324 machinery. R explains A.
t: Recall Article 324.

x: Both are true: VVPAT lets the voter check their vote because it prints a slip that stays visible for 7 seconds. R explains A.
t: Recall the 7-second VVPAT slip.

x: EVMs were first used on 19 May 1982, EPIC rolled out in 1993, VVPAT on 4 September 2013 and NOTA on 27 September 2013. The answer is a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii.
t: Recall the order: EVM 1982, EPIC 1993, VVPAT and NOTA 2013.

x: The EVM records and counts votes, EPIC provides photo ID, VVPAT gives a paper check, and NOTA is a negative-vote button. The answer is a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Match each device to its purpose.

x: Parur saw the first EVM, Noksen the first VVPAT, Goa the first all-EVM State poll (1999), and the 14th Lok Sabha poll (2004) the first all-EVM general election. The answer is a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
t: Recall each EVM and VVPAT first.

x: I and II are correct: EVMs are used for Lok Sabha and Assembly elections under the ECI's control. III is false because an EVM is a machine, not an electoral system.
t: Discriminate a voting machine from an electoral system.

x: A is true: NOTA came from the PUCL ruling of 2013. B is false because NOTA was ordered on 27 September 2013; 4 September is VVPAT's date.
t: Discriminate 4 September (VVPAT) from 27 September (NOTA).

x: A is true: Goa was the first State to hold an all-EVM Assembly election (1999). B is false because the 14th Lok Sabha election was in 2004.
t: Discriminate Goa's 1999 poll from the 2004 general election.

x: Three are correct: VVPAT came on 4 September 2013, NOTA on 27 September 2013, and Goa was the first all-EVM State poll. Statement 4 is false because the first all-EVM general election was 2004.
t: Discriminate Goa's 1999 poll from the 2004 general election.

x: Section 61A was added to the RPA, 1951 in 1989 to give EVMs legal backing, after the 1982 trial was challenged.
t: Recall the 1989 Section 61A.

x: Both are true: an EVM is a machine, not an electoral system, and India's system is first-past-the-post. The second fact does not explain the first, so R does not explain A.
t: Ask whether naming the system explains what a machine is.

x: Both are true: the first EVM trial, at Parur on 19 May 1982, gave rise to A.C. Jose v. Sivan Pillai. The date and place do not explain the case, so R does not explain A.
t: Ask whether a date and place explain a court case.

x: Two are purposes of EPIC: stopping bogus voting and impersonation. A paper slip is VVPAT's purpose and a negative button NOTA's.
t: Match each device to its purpose.

x: At least one-third of seats and chairperson posts in rural and urban local bodies must be reserved for women.
t: Recall the one-third baseline.

x: The minimum age to contest Panchayat or municipal elections is 21 (Articles 243F and 243V), compared with 25 for the Assembly.
t: Recall the ages 21, 25 and 30.

x: Option C is incorrect: the 106th Amendment excludes the Rajya Sabha and Legislative Councils. It covers the Lok Sabha, State Assemblies and the Delhi Assembly.
t: Remember that the Upper Houses are excluded.

x: Both are true: the reservation does not start at once because Article 334A ties it to the delimitation after the next census. R explains A.
t: Recall the census and delimitation precondition.

x: Both are true: the reservation lasts 15 years from its start, and Parliament can extend it. The power to extend does not explain the initial 15 years, so R does not explain A.
t: Ask whether an extension power explains the initial period.

x: Article 243D covers Panchayats, 243T municipalities, 330A the Lok Sabha, and 332A State Assemblies. The answer is a-iv, b-ii, c-iii, d-i.
t: Pair 330A (Lok Sabha) with 332A (Assemblies).

x: Panchayats come under the 73rd Amendment (1992), municipalities the 74th (1992), and the Lok Sabha and Assemblies the 106th (2023). The answer is a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv.
t: Match each level to its amendment.

x: Article 243D(2) gives the SC/ST women's sub-quota, 243D(3) one-third of direct seats, 243D(4) chairpersons' posts, and 334A rotation after delimitation. The answer is a-iii, b-ii, c-iv, d-i.
t: Recall the clauses of Article 243D.

x: I, II and III are correct: the 106th Amendment covers the Lok Sabha, State Assemblies and the Delhi Assembly. IV is false because the Rajya Sabha is excluded.
t: Remember that the Upper Houses are excluded.

x: I, II and III are correct: Article 243D(2) gives the SC/ST women's sub-quota, 243D(3) one-third of direct seats, and 243D(4) chairpersons' posts. IV is false because 243D is about Panchayats.
t: Recall the clauses of Article 243D.

x: Both are true: the constitutional minimum for women in Panchayats is one-third, and Bihar was the first State to raise it to 50%, in 2006.
t: Recall Bihar's 2006 lead.

x: Both are true: in Panchayats, the one-third reservation covers direct seats and chairpersons' posts, and in the Lok Sabha it covers general and SC/ST seats.
t: Compare what the women's quota covers at each level.

x: The 73rd and 74th Amendments came in 1992, Bihar's 50% in 2006, the 17th Lok Sabha's 78 women in 2019, and the 106th Amendment in 2023. The order is A, B, C, D.
t: Recall the years 1992, 2006, 2019 and 2023.

x: The 6th Lok Sabha (1977) had the fewest women, only 19 MPs.
t: Recall the 6th Lok Sabha's 19 women.

x: Both are true: the 17th Lok Sabha had the most women up to then because it had 78 women MPs, about 14.36%. R explains A.
t: Recall the 17th Lok Sabha's 78 women.

x: A is true: in the Delhi Assembly, the quota covers direct seats and SC and ST seats. B is false because Delhi comes under Article 239AA(2)(ba), not 332A.
t: Discriminate Article 332A (States) from 239AA (Delhi).

x: I, II and III are correct: Article 330A covers the Lok Sabha, 332A the Assemblies, and 239AA(2)(ba) Delhi. IV is false because 243T is municipalities, and the Rajya Sabha has no women's quota.
t: Pair each women's-quota Article with its House.

x: I, II and III are correct: the quota covers general and SC/ST seats in the Lok Sabha and Assemblies, and direct and SC/ST seats in Delhi. IV is false because the Rajya Sabha is excluded.
t: Remember that the Upper Houses are excluded.

x: The 6th Lok Sabha was 1977, the 73rd and 74th Amendments 1992, Bihar's 50% 2006, and the 17th Lok Sabha 2019. The answer is a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i.
t: Recall the years 1977, 1992, 2006 and 2019.

x: The Lok Sabha quota covers total seats including SC/ST ones, the State quota general and SC/ST seats, and the Delhi quota direct and SC/ST seats. The Upper Houses are excluded. The answer is a-iv, b-ii, c-iii, d-i.
t: Remember that the Upper Houses are excluded.

x: All four are correct: Panchayats come under Article 243D and the 73rd Amendment, and municipalities under 243T and the 74th, both of 1992.
t: Pair Article 243D (Panchayats) with 243T (municipalities).

x: In the Delhi Assembly, the 106th Amendment reserves at least one-third of all seats, direct and SC/ST, for women.
t: Recall the one-third quota for Delhi.

x: The Rajya Sabha and the Legislative Councils are excluded from the 106th Amendment and have no women's reservation.
t: Remember that the Upper Houses are excluded.

x: The 106th Amendment Act, 2023, the women's reservation law, is called the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam.
t: Recall the 106th Amendment's name.

x: Both are true: Article 243T(3) reserves one-third of municipal seats for women and 243T(4) one-third of chairpersons' posts. Two parallel clauses do not explain each other, so R does not explain A.
t: Ask whether two parallel clauses explain each other.
